title: Oasis Two: the extreme one, three peaks and a hundred factorial
summary: They teach the family to hunt the biggest and the smallest at the whiteboard and then run a puzzle table on it, climb one peak each over roots, the geometry block and scientific notation, and give the month 2 monster its ending.
materials: the field journal, open at this sprint's extremal pages
whiteboard and marker, wiped clean before anybody sits down
a sheet ruled into four rows of four boxes, for the last table problem
the desert wall map, for the second oasis flag
chairs for everybody, because the table problems belong to the room
twelve slips of paper and a pen, for the ring problem

steps.title: How the second oasis runs
steps.body:
The second shade of the season, and the first one you reach with a crossing behind you.

Today runs in three parts.

First the whiteboard. Before those three problems, teach them the trailing-zeros puzzle you invented in week 7: your own range of numbers, your own count of the zeros, proved by counting every five and checking each one for a hidden second five. Say the idea's name out loud as you explain it: the scarce ingredient decides the answer, not the plentiful one. Walk them through your own proof, then teach it well enough that they could set their own trailing-zeros puzzle.

Then teach the family the tool this sprint gave you: stare at the biggest, the smallest, the nearest or the first, because the extreme one has nowhere to hide. Teach it before you use it, in your own words, and then put three problems in front of the room and let them try. They will want to test cases. Let them, and then show them what looking at the extreme does instead.

Then the summit: three peaks, one for each week of the sprint. Peak 1 is square roots, exact and estimated and tidied up. Peak 2 is the geometry block, where the answer is only half the work and the reason written beside it is the other half. Peak 3 is scientific notation, the zoom lever. Each peak ends on a problem built to be harder than the ones before it.

Then the month 2 monster gets its ending. A hundred factorial, and the zeros on the end of it. Today it either cracks or it gets retired with honours, and both of those are respectable endings. Only pretending counts as failing.

A climb is not a test. If a summit problem slows you down, that is the desert doing its job and not a mark against you. Keep the field journal open the whole way, and on every geometry step write the reason in the margin before you write the next line, even when the reason feels too obvious to say.

steps.title: The family table: the extreme one has nowhere to hide

problems.prompt: Twelve people stand in a ring and each one writes a whole number on a slip of paper. Every single person's number turns out to be exactly the average of the two numbers beside them, left neighbour and right neighbour. The largest number anybody wrote is 30. What is the smallest number anybody wrote?
explanation: Do not start with a random person. Start with whoever wrote the largest number.
That number is the average of its two neighbours, so those two add up to twice it.
Neither neighbour can beat the largest. Two numbers that cannot beat it and still add to twice it must both equal it.
So both neighbours are largest too, and the same argument steps round the ring seat by seat.
It comes all the way round, so every slip carries the same number.
problems.useAgain: when everything in a problem leans on its neighbours and there is no obvious place to begin.
hints: Twelve people is too many to start with. Is there one person you know something about before you know anything about the rest?
Take the biggest number in the ring and write down what being an average forces on its two neighbours.
problems.socraticHint: If a number is the average of two others, can both of those others be smaller than it?

variant.prompt: Now nine people stand in the ring and the rule is the same: every number is the average of the two beside it. The largest number written is 14. What is the smallest?

problems.prompt: Twelve people stand for a photo in a grid, three rows of four. In each row find the tallest person, then out of those three row winners find the shortest one and call her A. Now in each column find the shortest person, then out of those four column winners find the tallest one and call him B. True or false: A can never be shorter than B.
explanation: Do not test grids. Draw one, mark A's row and B's column, and look at the person standing where they cross.
A is the tallest in that row, so A is at least as tall as the crossing person.
B is the shortest in that column, so the crossing person is at least as tall as B.
Chain those two and A is at least as tall as B.
Nobody was measured. One person, standing where the two extremes meet, settled the whole grid.
problems.useAgain: when two extreme choices are made in different directions and you are asked which one wins.
hints: Do not try lots of grids. Draw one, and mark the row A came out of and the column B came out of.
Exactly one person stands in both A's row and B's column. Say what A knows about that person, then what B knows.
problems.socraticHint: Is there anybody in the photo that both A and B are entitled to an opinion about?

variant.prompt: The same photo grid, the same A and the same B. True or false: B can never be shorter than A.

problems.prompt: Rule a grid of four rows and four columns, then write the numbers 1 to 16 into the sixteen boxes, each number used once. Add up each row, which gives four row totals. Whoever fills the grid is trying to make the largest of those four totals as small as it will go. What is the smallest that the largest row total can possibly be?
explanation: The numbers 1 to 16 add up to 136 whatever the order, and the four row totals share that out.
Suppose every row came in at 33 or less. Four such rows carry only 132, short of 136.
So some row reaches 34 however cleverly the boxes are filled. That is the extreme talking.
A bound is only half an answer. It says what cannot happen, not that anything can.
Fill the grid so all four rows total 34, and the other half is done. Such fillings exist.
problems.useAgain: when a question asks for the smallest possible largest thing, or the largest possible smallest thing.
hints: You cannot try every filling. Ask what the four row totals add up to before you place a single number.
Suppose every row came in under some total, and see what that would do to the sum of all sixteen numbers.
problems.socraticHint: Whatever order the numbers go in, what do the four row totals always add up to?

variant.prompt: Now a grid of three rows and three columns holding the numbers 1 to 9, each used once, giving three row totals. What is the smallest that the largest row total can possibly be?

steps.title: Teach the extreme, then run the table
steps.prompt:
Whiteboard, family sitting down, marker in your hand.

Teach the tool before you use it, and teach it the way you met it rather than the way a book would. Say what it is in one sentence: when a problem is full of things you cannot see, look at the biggest one, or the smallest, or the nearest, or the first, because the extreme one has nowhere left to hide. It cannot pass the problem sideways to a neighbour, because past it there is no neighbour.

Then show why that is worth anything, using the ring of twelve. Ask the room to try the ring with actual numbers, because that is what everybody does first. Let it run long enough to become annoying. Then put a slip in the largest person's hand and ask the one question that ends it: what does being an average force onto their two neighbours, when neither neighbour is allowed to be bigger?

Then run the table. Problem one, then two, then three, and after each one the family gets to try before you say anything at all. Hand out paper. A wrong start somebody made themselves is worth more than a right answer they watched you make.

One honest thing to say out loud while you have them, because it is the part people skip. The extremal principle tells you where to stand, not what to say when you get there. In the ring it hands you the whole answer. In the grid of sixteen boxes it hands you half, a promise about what cannot happen, and you still have to build a real filling to finish the job. A tool that gets you halfway is still a tool. Pretending it got you all the way is the mirage.

Finish on the invitation: ask the room for a problem they think the tool cannot touch, and write it into the field journal whether or not you can crack it today.

steps.title: Summit: three peaks over the sprint

problems.prompt: Peak 1a, roots. A square patio is paved with square tiles, all the same size, laid as a full square with none cut and none left over. It takes 289 tiles altogether. How many tiles run along one edge?
explanation: A square patio holds the same count along every edge, so that number times itself gives the total.
Bracket it first. Ten tens make 100 and twenty twenties make 400, so the edge is between ten and twenty.
289 ends in a 9, so the edge ends in 3 or 7.
The one ending in 7 lands on 289 exactly.
problems.useAgain: when a square total is given and you want the length of one of its sides back.
hints: A square patio has the same count along every edge, so one number multiplied by itself makes the whole thing.
Bracket it before you hunt: which two tens does the edge sit between?
problems.socraticHint: 289 ends in a 9. Which single digits, multiplied by themselves, end in a 9?

variant.prompt: A second square patio is laid the same way and takes 529 tiles. How many tiles run along one edge?

problems.prompt: Peak 1b, roots. The square root of 770 is not a whole number. Which pair of whole numbers does it sit between?
explanation: Do not reach for a decimal. Climb the perfect squares until one of them steps over 770.
27 times 27 makes 729, just under, and 28 times 28 makes 784, just over.
Squaring keeps order, so a number caught between those two squares has its root caught between those two whole numbers.
770 sits much nearer 784 than 729, so the root is just under the higher one.
problems.useAgain: when a root is not exact and you need to place it on the line rather than name it.
hints: Do not estimate the root itself. List the perfect squares climbing up past 770.
Find the largest perfect square under 770, then the smallest one over it.
problems.socraticHint: If one number is bigger than another, is its square always bigger too?

variant.prompt: And the square root of 1,150. Which pair of whole numbers does that one sit between?

problems.prompt: Peak 1c, roots tidied. The square root of 320 can be written as a whole number multiplied by the square root of a smaller whole number, with the number left under the root made as small as it will go. What is the whole number out in front?
explanation: Split 320 into the biggest perfect square you can find, times what is left.
320 is 64 times 5, and 64 is a perfect square while 5 hides none.
The root of a product is the product of the roots, so the root of 64 steps out in front.
Splitting 320 as 4 times 80 does not finish, because 80 still hides a 16.
problems.useAgain: when a root looks untidy and you want the smallest possible number left under the sign.
hints: Do not compute a decimal. Look for square factors hiding inside 320.
List the perfect squares and test which of them divide 320, then take the largest that does.
problems.socraticHint: Which perfect squares divide 320 exactly, and which of those is the biggest?

variant.prompt: Now the square root of 242, written the same way, with the number under the root made as small as it will go. What is the whole number out in front?

problems.prompt: Peak 2a, angles, and the reason goes in the margin beside every step. Two straight roads cross at a junction, making four angles. The angle on the north-east side of the crossing measures 43 degrees. The angle on the north-west side sits next to it along the same straight road. How many degrees is the north-west angle?
explanation: The two angles sit side by side along one straight road, so together they cover a straight line.
A straight line holds 180 degrees. That is the reason, and it goes in the margin.
So the north-west angle is 180 take away 43.
The angle straight across the junction is not beside it, and that one stays at 43.
problems.useAgain: when two angles sit side by side along one straight line and only one of them is given.
hints: Ask which of the four angles shares a straight road with the one you were handed.
Two angles along a straight line are not free to be anything at all. Write down what they must come to together.
problems.socraticHint: What would those two angles make together if you rubbed out the line standing between them?

variant.prompt: At a second junction the north-east angle measures 58 degrees. How many degrees is the north-west angle beside it?

problems.prompt: Peak 2b, angle sums, the torn corners of season 2 grown up. A paving stone is a regular pentagon: five equal sides and five equal corners. How many degrees is each of its inside corners?
explanation: Draw lines from one corner to all the others. That cuts the pentagon into triangles.
Five sides give three triangles, each holding 180 degrees, so the corners hold 540 degrees altogether.
Regular means all five corners are equal, so share the 540 out between them.
The trap is dividing 180 by five. The 180 belongs to a triangle, not to the stone.
problems.useAgain: when a many-sided shape is regular and you want the size of one corner.
hints: Do not guess from the picture. Chop the pentagon into triangles by drawing from one single corner.
Count the triangles that gives you, then use what one triangle's corners always come to.
problems.socraticHint: A triangle's corners always come to the same total. Can a pentagon be built out of triangles?

variant.prompt: A second paving stone is a regular dodecagon, twelve equal sides. How many degrees is each of its inside corners?

problems.prompt: Peak 2c, the theorem you cut out and rearranged. A triangular garden bed has sides of 8 feet, 15 feet and 17 feet. True or false: one of its corners is a perfect right angle.
explanation: Only a right angle makes the two squares on the short sides exactly fill the square on the longest.
So square the short sides: 8 times 8 is 64, and 15 times 15 is 225.
Those add to 289, and 17 times 17 is 289 too, so that corner is square.
Measuring a drawing would not settle it. A sketch that looks right is a mirage.
problems.useAgain: when three side lengths are given and you want to know whether a corner is truly square.
hints: Do not measure a drawing. The longest side has a job of its own in this test.
Square the two shorter sides and add them, then compare that with the square of the longest side.
problems.socraticHint: If the two small squares came out bigger than the big one, what would that corner have to be doing?

variant.prompt: A second bed has sides of 6 feet, 8 feet and 11 feet. True or false: one of its corners is a perfect right angle.

problems.prompt: Peak 2d, distance. On the jumbo-chalk grid on the driveway, one flag stands at 2 across and 3 up, and another stands at 14 across and 8 up. Each square of the grid is one step wide. How many steps long is the straight line from one flag to the other?
explanation: Walk it the boring way first: 12 steps across from 2 to 14, then 5 steps up.
Those two walks are the short sides of a right triangle whose long side is the answer.
Square and add: 144 and 25 make 169, whose root is the long side.
Do not mix the coordinates crossways. Across with across, up with up.
problems.useAgain: when two points are given by their coordinates and you want the real distance between them.
hints: Do not reach for a ruler. Get from one flag to the other in two straight walks, one across and one up.
Those two walks are the short sides of a right triangle, and its long side is what you were asked for.
problems.socraticHint: Which two moves would a rook make to get from one flag to the other, and what shape do those two moves draw?

variant.prompt: Two more flags, one at 3 across and 1 up, the other at 27 across and 8 up. How many steps long is the straight line between them?

problems.prompt: Peak 3a, the zoom lever. Written in scientific notation, 4,700,000 becomes 4.7 multiplied by 10 raised to some power. What is that power?
explanation: Scientific notation allows one digit in front of the point, so it lands just after the 4.
In the plain number the point sits at the far right, after the last zero.
Count the places the point travels to its new home, and that count is the power.
Check by multiplying back: 4.7 lots of a million rebuilds the number exactly.
problems.useAgain: when a number is too long to read and you want it said as one digit and a power of ten.
hints: Scientific notation allows exactly one digit in front of the point. Where does that put the point in this number?
Mark where the point starts and where it has to end up, then count the places in between.
problems.socraticHint: Does moving the point one place to the left make a number ten times bigger or ten times smaller?

variant.prompt: And 0.00082, written as 8.2 multiplied by 10 raised to some power. What is that power?

problems.prompt: Peak 3b. A grain of sand measures about 5 x 10 to the power of negative 4 meters across. Suppose you laid 2 x 10 to the 6th grains of sand in one long row, touching end to end. How many meters long is the row?
explanation: Multiplying here splits into two jobs: the front numbers, then the powers of ten.
The front numbers give 5 times 2, which is 10.
The powers add their exponents: negative 4 plus 6 gives ten squared.
So the row is 10 lots of ten squared, which is ten lots of a hundred.
Nobody writes the zeros out. Only the exponent changes.
problems.useAgain: when two numbers in scientific notation are multiplied and you want the answer without writing the zeros out.
hints: Do not write either number out in full. Treat the front numbers and the powers of ten as two separate jobs.
When powers of the same base are multiplied, something happens to the exponents. Do that part first.
problems.socraticHint: Which of the two exponents is pulling the answer down, and which is pushing it up?

variant.prompt: Suppose the grains measure 3 x 10 to the power of negative 3 meters across and you lay 4 x 10 to the 5th of them in a row. How many meters long is that row?

problems.prompt: Peak 3c, and this one is a mirage hunt. Four distances are written below, and not all of them have been tidied into proper scientific notation. Which is the largest?
explanation: The front numbers must be tidied before the exponents can be compared.
70 x 10 to the 4th becomes 7 x 10 to the 5th.
And 0.9 x 10 to the 7th becomes 9 x 10 to the 6th.
Now two sit at ten to the 5th and two at ten to the 6th, and 9 beats 6.
So the smallest-looking front number is the largest of all.
problems.useAgain: when numbers written with powers of ten are compared and the front numbers are not all in the same shape.
hints: The biggest exponent does not win automatically. Two of these four are not in proper scientific notation yet.
Rewrite each one so exactly one digit sits in front of the point, then compare the powers.
problems.socraticHint: Which of these four have a front number that proper scientific notation would not allow?

variant.prompt: And these four distances. Which is the largest?

problems.prompt: The month 2 monster gets its ending. A hundred factorial means every whole number from 1 up to 100 multiplied together, and it is a number nobody in this house is going to write out. How many zeros does it end in, and why exactly that many? Write the count and the argument that makes the count certain, in your own words, the way you would say it standing at the whiteboard.

mustMention: a zero on the end comes from a ten, and a ten is a two meeting a five
there are far more twos than fives, so the fives are the scarce ingredient
twenty numbers up to a hundred carry a five, and the four multiples of twenty-five carry a second one

explanation: Start with what a trailing zero actually is. A number ends in a zero exactly when ten divides it, and it gains another zero for each extra ten.
Ten is not an atom. Ten is two times five, so every trailing zero costs one two and one five out of the product.
So the real question is how many pairs of a two and a five hide inside the numbers up to a hundred. Twos turn up in every second number, so the fives are what run out.
Count the fives. Twenty of the numbers from 1 to 100 are multiples of five, which is 5, 10, 15 and on up to 100.
Now the trap that made this a monster. 25, 50, 75 and 100 are each five times five, so each hides a second five that the first count walked past. That is four more.
Twenty plus four is twenty-four fives, and the twos are nowhere near that scarce. Exactly twenty-four tens can be built, so a hundred factorial ends in twenty-four zeros and not one more.
problems.useAgain: when a question asks how many times something divides a huge product and multiplying it out is impossible.
hints: Do not think about zeros yet. Think about what has to happen inside a number for a zero to appear on its end at all.
Ten breaks into a two and a five. Count how many of each the numbers 1 to 100 hand you, and see which one runs short first.
problems.socraticHint: Of the two ingredients in a ten, which one do you expect to run out first, and how could you check that hunch?

steps.title: Explain it
steps.prompt:
Write the ending of the factorial zeros monster for somebody who has never heard the word factorial, one idea per sentence.

Start where you started, with a small case you could actually see. Ten factorial, or fifteen, worked far enough to watch the zeros arrive. Then the move that turns a pattern into a reason: a zero on the end is a ten, a ten is a two meeting a five, and one of those two is much harder to find than the other. Then the count. Then the twenty-fives, because that is the sentence your reader will need most and the one you would have walked past a fortnight ago.

Put the number at the end, where your reader can arrive at it the way you did.

If the crack never came today, write that instead, and write down exactly which step stopped making sense to you. That sentence is worth more to the next person than a borrowed answer, and this monster retires with honours either way.
